passage: Sarika, you're doing it again, saying yes to everyone. Sit, I'll tell you what happened to your Lavanya Mami at your age. At twenty-five I cooked for my in-laws, tutored my cousin's son, ran my friends' errands and worked full-time at the bank. Everyone called me the helpful one. I liked it. Then one night at a wedding I fainted, just from being empty. The doctor said I needed rest. Lying there, I understood: if I break, nobody gets help from me at all. So I learned a small word. No. "No, not this Sunday." "No, I can't tutor this month, but here's a friend who can." I still help, beta. Just not until I'm hollow. Now, drink this, and tell your manager no.

qa.a: At a wedding.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel about being called the helpful one, before the fainting?
qa.a: Lavanya liked being called the helpful one and enjoyed it, which made it harder to notice how empty she was getting.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Lavanya, and what changed afterwards?
qa.a: Fainting at the wedding showed that if she broke, nobody would be helped, so she started saying no sometimes while still helping.

qa.q: How might Sarika hear this story from Lavanya Mami?
qa.a: Sarika may feel understood and gently warned, seeing that saying no to a manager doesn't mean Sarika stops being kind.

passage: Yogesh had worked double shifts at the hospital lab all week, and his eyes felt full of sand. On Saturday night, as rain hammered the window, Dhruv called. "Bro, can you help me shift flats tomorrow? Six a.m. The truck's booked." Yogesh always said yes. He'd helped Dhruv move twice already, and fixed his mother's fan last month. He opened his mouth to say yes again, then felt how heavy his arms were. "Dhruv, I can't tomorrow. I'm wrecked. If I carry your fridge like this, I'll drop it on my foot." Silence. "But I'll come Wednesday evening and help you unpack and set up the kitchen. Promise." Dhruv sighed, then laughed. "Fine. Bring the good screwdriver." Yogesh slept eleven hours.

qa.a: Yogesh slept eleven hours.

qa.q: What made Yogesh hesitate before saying yes again?
qa.a: He felt how heavy his arms were and how exhausted he was, and worried he could not help safely in that state.

qa.q: Which choice kept Yogesh both kind and rested?
qa.a: He said no to Sunday but offered Wednesday evening for unpacking, which protected his rest while still showing he cared.

qa.q: How does Dhruv seem to take Yogesh's no?
qa.a: Dhruv is a bit disappointed at first, shown by the silence and sigh, but accepts it with a laugh because help is still coming.

passage: For a month Sabina had cooked lunch for her uncle's family after his surgery, dropped her nieces to tuition and answered every call from her office at night. On Thursday her brother Bhupen came to her Kolkata flat with a cardboard box. "The kids have a science model due Monday. You're so good at these." Sabina looked at the box, then at the clock: nine-forty. Her head throbbed. "Bhupen, I love them. I'll help on Sunday for one hour, to show them how. But I won't make it for them, and not tonight." He blinked. "You never say no." "I know. That's the problem." After he left, she made tea, sat on the balcony and watched the tram lights pass. She felt guilty for ten minutes. Then she felt lighter.

qa.a: A cardboard box for the kids' science model.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel after Bhupen left?
qa.a: She felt guilty for ten minutes, and then she felt lighter.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see his sister after she says no?
qa.a: Bhupen is surprised because she never refused before, but he may start to notice how much she has been carrying.

passage:
"Parveen Apa, just tonight? Please?" Imran stood in the doorway with his baby son on his hip. "We have Rubina's cousin's wedding. You're so good with him."
Parveen was still in her office clothes, her feet aching. "Imran, I babysat Tuesday and Thursday. I've been up since five."
"But you always say yes."
"I know." She took a breath. "And that's why I'm saying no tonight. If I keep saying yes when I'm this tired, I'll start snapping at you all, and I don't want that."
Imran's face fell. "So what do I do?"
"Ask Ammi. Or take him along; he sleeps anywhere." She reached out and stroked the baby's cheek. "But Saturday morning, I'm free. You two go for breakfast, and I'll keep him till lunch. Properly, happily."
Imran was quiet, then grinned a little. "Properly, happily. Deal."

qa.q: When is Parveen free to look after the baby?
qa.a: On Saturday morning, till lunch.

qa.q: Why did Parveen take a breath before saying no?
qa.a: She felt the pull to say yes as always, and needed a moment to hold her ground because she was exhausted and worried she would start snapping.

qa.q: What choice did Parveen make, and why is it a caring one?
qa.a: She said no tonight but offered Saturday morning, so her help comes from real energy instead of emptying her until she resents it.

qa.q: How might Imran see his sister's no?
qa.a: He is disappointed at first because he is used to her always saying yes, but her Saturday offer helps him see she still wants to help.

grounding: It shows an adult who helps her family generously but says no when exhausted, knowing that kindness which empties the giver cannot last.

passage:
I'm Keerthana, and a year ago I was the friend everyone called, the good girl who never said no. Need a ride to the airport at four? Keerthana. Need someone to cover a shift, fix a CV, babysit a dog? Keerthana. I loved being needed. I'm not ashamed of that.
But last March I got so tired I cried in the office washroom because someone asked me to proofread a two-line email. That scared me.
So I started saying something I'd never said: "Not this week, but I can do next Tuesday." The first time, my hands were sweating. My friend Ayesha just said, "Oh, okay," and found someone else. Nothing broke.
When Ayesha moved flats in June, I was rested, and I spent the whole Sunday packing her kitchen, laughing over her twelve identical mugs. I helped more that day than I would have in a month of exhausted yeses.
I still say yes a lot. Just not to everything.

qa.q: What was Keerthana asked to proofread when she cried in the washroom?
qa.a: A two-line email.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel the first time she said 'not this week'?
qa.a: She was nervous, with sweating hands, afraid that saying no would upset people or break something.

qa.q: What turning point changed Keerthana's habits, and what did she choose after it?
qa.a: Crying over a tiny request scared her into seeing she was empty, so she began offering later dates instead of always saying yes at once.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have experienced Keerthana's change?
qa.a: Ayesha took the first no easily and later got a rested, cheerful friend who spent a whole Sunday helping her move.

grounding: It shows an adult who used to help everyone and learns to say no when exhausted, so her generous care can last.

passage:
Supervisor's note, hospital ward, 18 June.
Pradeep has covered three extra night shifts for colleagues this month, and drives his cousins to the airport on weekends. Everybody asks Pradeep.
Today, at the end of a double shift, Keerthana asked him to swap Saturday. I watched. He paused, rubbed his eyes, and said, "Not this time, Keerthana. I'm running on empty. Next week I can help."
She looked surprised, then nodded. "Fair. You look finished."
I was glad. Pradeep has been quieter lately, less patient with patients' families. He was giving until nothing was left.
What I did next: I made sure the Saturday swap went to the relief pool, and told Pradeep that saying no is part of doing this job well for years, not just months.

qa.q: How many extra night shifts had Pradeep covered this month?
qa.a: Three extra night shifts.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he rubbed his eyes before answering?
qa.a: He felt exhausted and a little torn, wanting to help but knowing he had nothing left.

qa.q: What did the note-writer do next, and why does it help?
qa.a: They sent the swap to the relief pool and told Pradeep that saying no is part of lasting in the job, supporting his limit.

qa.q: How does Keerthana seem to take Pradeep's no?
qa.a: She seems surprised at first but then understands, seeing he looks worn out.

grounding: It shows an adult who helps generously but says no when exhausted, as noted by a supervisor.

passage:
Saturday
Tejas called at eight: "Can you help me shift flats tomorrow? The truck's at seven."
Every part of me wanted to say yes. He's my little brother. I always say yes. Last month I spent both weekends painting his old flat.
But I've worked six days straight and I'm so tired my eyes hurt. Tomorrow is the only day I have to sleep, do my laundry and call Nani.
So I said, "Tejas, not tomorrow. I'm wiped out. I'll come next Saturday and help you unpack and set up the kitchen."
He was quiet, then said, "Okay. Fair." I felt guilty for about ten minutes. Then I felt okay.
I can't help anyone if I'm empty.
– Gurpreet

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel after saying no?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt guilty for about ten minutes, then okay and at peace with it.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel about the no?
qa.a: He might be disappointed at first, but he seems to understand, saying "Okay. Fair."

passage:
In the village near Nashik, everyone called Santosh when something went wrong. He fixed pumps, drove the old van to the hospital at night, and filled in forms for neighbours.
This harvest week he had worked eighteen-hour days. On Thursday night his cousin Pankaj called: "Can you drive my in-laws to the station at four in the morning?"
Santosh felt his whole body sag. He wanted to say yes. He always said yes.
"Pankaj, I can't tonight. I'm finished. I'll lend you the van keys, or ask Rakesh, he's free."
There was a silence. Then Pankaj said, "Okay, bhau. You sleep."
Santosh lay down, guilty for a minute, then relieved. The next morning he woke rested and helped three people before noon.

qa.q: What time did Pankaj want his in-laws driven to the station?
qa.a: At four in the morning.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel after saying no to Pankaj?
qa.a: He felt guilty for a minute, then relieved, because he was exhausted and needed rest.

qa.q: Why was Santosh's way of saying no a good choice?
qa.a: He said no honestly but offered other help, the van keys or Rakesh, and resting meant he could help three people the next day.

qa.q: How does Pankaj seem to take Santosh's refusal?
qa.a: After a short silence Pankaj accepts it kindly, telling him to sleep.

grounding: An adult who helps everyone generously says no when exhausted, knowing that care that empties him cannot last.

passage:
Javier was the one his friends in Madrid always called. He helped Mei move flat twice, sat up with his brother after his breakup, and cooked for his grandmother every Sunday.
This month he had a big exam at the architecture firm and was sleeping five hours a night. When Mei texted, "Could you help me paint my new place this weekend? 🙏", he felt his chest tighten.
He typed "Of course!" and then deleted it.
He wrote: "I really want to, but I'm running on empty. Can I bring lunch on Sunday instead, and paint next weekend?"
Mei replied, "Of course! Thanks for being honest. 😊"
Javier put the phone down and felt lighter. He still cooked for his grandmother. He just skipped one weekend of painting.

qa.q: How many hours a night was Javier sleeping?
qa.a: He was sleeping five hours a night.

qa.q: What did Javier feel when Mei asked for help painting?
qa.a: He felt his chest tighten, torn between wanting to help and being exhausted.

qa.q: How did Mei take Javier's honest answer?
qa.a: Mei was understanding and grateful for his honesty, not hurt.

passage:
At the community health centre in Guntur, nurse Leela was known as the one who never left. She covered shifts, held babies for tired mothers and stayed late to explain medicines.
On Friday her colleague Siddharth asked, "Leela, could you take my Sunday night? My cousin's engagement."
Leela had already worked six days. Her back ached and she'd snapped at her own sister that morning.
She took a breath. "Siddharth, I'd like to help, but I'm too tired. If I take it, I'll be no good to anyone on Monday."
He looked surprised, then nodded. "Fair. I'll ask the pool."
Leela went home, slept twelve hours and called her sister to apologise. On Monday she was the first to hold a crying baby again.

qa.q: How many days had Leela already worked?
qa.a: She had already worked six days.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when she decided to refuse Siddharth?
qa.a: She was tired and aching, a little guilty, but clear that she needed rest to keep caring for others.

qa.q: What did Leela's rest make possible?
qa.a: She could apologise to her sister and return on Monday ready to care for patients again.

qa.q: How does Siddharth respond to Leela's refusal?
qa.a: He is surprised at first but accepts it as fair and asks the pool instead.

grounding: An adult nurse who helps generously says no when exhausted, knowing that care that empties her cannot last.

passage:
Dear Nirmala Didi,
Thank you for thinking of me for Chinnu's wedding shopping. You know I love that girl, and I've loved doing the lists and tailor runs for every cousin so far. This time I have to say no to the full job. The last three weekends I've driven Amma to her physio, covered double shifts at the hospital and helped Raju move flats. On Sunday I fell asleep standing at the stove. I don't want to show up for Chinnu grumpy and half-present.
What I can do: the jewellery trip on the 14th, and I'll send you my tailor's number tonight. The rest I'm handing back, with love. I'd rather be useful for years than burnt out by March.
Your Minakshi

passage: You asked what I've learned this year. Okay, here's one. I'm Akash, and for about three years I was everyone's free tech support. Chacha's printer, my cousin's laptop, my friend Nandini's router: every Sunday, gone. I liked being needed, I really did. Then in March, after a month of late nights at work, Nandini called: could I help her shift flats that Sunday? My stomach dropped. I heard myself say, 'I can't this weekend, I'm running on empty. I'll bring dinner to your new place on Saturday and set up the wifi then.' There was a pause, and then she said, 'Oh, thank God, I thought you'd never say no to anything.' We laughed. I slept eleven hours that Sunday. And the Saturday dinner was actually fun, because I wasn't resentful.

qa.q: What did Akash offer Nandini instead of helping on Sunday?
qa.a: To bring dinner to the new place on Saturday and set up the wifi then.

qa.q: What did Akash's stomach dropping suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Akash felt dread and exhaustion at one more request, torn between liking being needed and having nothing left to give.

qa.q: What could Akash do next time a relative asks for weekend tech help?
qa.a: Akash could check energy first and offer a specific time that fits, instead of saying yes automatically out of habit.

qa.q: How does Nandini see Akash's no?
qa.a: She sees it as a relief and a healthy sign, since she had worried Akash never said no to anything 🙂

passage: I share a desk row with Payal at the insurance office, so I see a lot. She is the one who covers your shift when your kid is sick, who remembers birthdays, who drove the new trainee to the station in the rain. Last Friday our manager asked her to stay late again to finish someone else's claims. I watched her rub her eyes, then smile and say, 'Not tonight. I've stayed late four days this week and I'm starting to make mistakes. I can take two of them first thing Monday.' The manager blinked, then nodded. On Monday she came in early, finished both, and brought samosas for the team. I don't know what went on in her head. But I'm Vaibhav, the one who never says no, and I left at six that Friday too.

Tuesday. She got home at ten after a twelve-hour shift at the hospital billing desk, feet throbbing. Tushar called. "Can you come over and help me with the gas connection form? Tonight?"
Pallavi closed her eyes. The old Pallavi would have grabbed her keys. "Not tonight, Tushar. I'm completely wiped out. Thursday after seven, I'm all yours."
A pause. "Okay. Thursday."
Thursday. Rested, she filled the form in fifteen minutes, and they ate instant noodles on his new balcony, laughing about the tempo driver.
